This excerpt provides experimental and simulation evidence relevant to plate inclination and vibration-mode effects, but it does not establish where a melt stream should strike the plate—near its center or edge—or whether impact should be placed specifically at an antinode or nodal point. The apparatus used an adjustable inclined vibrating surface, specifically a 160 mm × 30 mm × 1 mm stainless-steel plate. Simulations compared 30°, 45°, and 60° inclinations after 0.004 s. The measured remaining-liquid fractions were 48.2%, 49.7%, and 50.9%, respectively, so the extreme-angle difference was only 2.7%; the authors therefore considered inclination’s effect on atomization of one droplet insignificant, while noting that it could matter for larger feed rates, stand geometry, and heat transfer. The experiment did observe that residual liquid formed a pattern corresponding to the plate’s nodes and antinodes, demonstrating that the vibration mode affects liquid retention and distribution. The excerpt contains no instructions or evidence concerning regular abrasive cleaning, removal of adherent metal, or replacing plates between runs. It also does not identify a preferred stream-impact location relative to the center or edge. Those apparatus-design and maintenance recommendations would need to be supported by other published documents or sections not included here.

## pqac-00000021

From text 'kustron2023developmentofhighpower pages 4-7'.

Pawel Kustron, Marcin Korzeniowski, Adam Sajbura, Tomasz Piwowarczyk, Pawel Kaczynski, and Pawel Sokolowski. Development of high-power ultrasonic system dedicated to metal powder atomization. Applied Sciences, 13:8984, Aug 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/app13158984, doi:10.3390/app13158984. This article has 44 citations.

Kustron et al. (2023) describe the melt stream as being directed onto the surface of the vibrating plate coupled to the ultrasonic transducer. The plate diameter was selected to capture as much of the converging molten stream as possible, rather than specifying that impact should occur at the center or edge. Their design objective was also to maintain high and uniform vibration amplitude across the working surface. The numerical analysis explicitly distinguishes nodal points, where amplitude is zero, from locations of maximum deflection; therefore, the excerpt supports avoiding nodal points for effective atomization, but it does not identify a preferred center-versus-edge impact position. The authors modeled plates with diameters of 60, 108, 140, and 190 mm, corresponding to one through four nodal-point configurations at approximately 20 kHz, and reported maximum deflection amplitudes for each design. This excerpt contains no instructions concerning plate inclination angle, abrasive cleaning, removal of adherent metal, or replacing plates between runs. It likewise provides no experimental evidence on those maintenance procedures. Such claims would require consulting other apparatus-design or experimental-method documents rather than relying on this passage.

## pqac-00000022

From text 'szostakstaropietka2025influenceofprocess pages 11-13'.

Rafał Szostak-Staropiętka, Wojciech Presz, Roksana Pawlic, Anna Dziubińska, and Katarzyna Kołacz. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/metrology5030039, doi:10.3390/metrology5030039. This article has 0 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt from Szostak-Staropiętka et al. (2025) provides experimental evidence about vibration amplitude and locations of atomization on a vibrating plate, but it does not describe a published metal-melt apparatus design in sufficient detail to answer all parts of the question. In the experiment, the initial measured maximum amplitude was only about 2.8 µm, which was insufficient to initiate atomization; after amplifier settings were rearranged, an amplitude of 8 µm was reached and atomization proceeded smoothly. The authors observed that atomization was strongest at the nodes of the vibrating plate, rather than at antinodes. For a liquid with viscosity 7.5 mPa·s, density 997 kg/m³, and surface tension 0.055 N/m, the required amplitude was at least 8 µm. The excerpt does not state whether a melt stream should strike near the center or edge of the plate, nor does it provide instructions concerning plate inclination angle, regular abrasive cleaning, removal of adherent metal, or replacing plates between runs. It also concerns liquid atomization experiments and simulations, not powder characterization. The paper’s conclusion supports ultrasonic atomization as potentially applicable to testing liquid properties, including liquid metals, while emphasizing that simulations can identify experimental problems such as overestimated output amplitude.

                   A laboratory shaker was used to separate the different powder fractions, together
                         with a set of sieves with the appropriate mesh size. After all 16 sieving cycles had been
                          completed, it was found that fraction 2 (containing particles between 80 µm and 50 µm
                              in size) accounted for 48% to 56% of the total weight of the material produced. Fraction 3
                             (containing particles < 50 µm in size) accounted for 30% to 42% of the total mass of material
                           produced. The atomisation process should also be assessed by the percentage of the F1 and
                          waste fractions. Minimising the proportion of these fractions, especially waste, is important,
                            as they will not be used in further technological processes. This criterion is best met by
                       powders produced according to strategies S6_100_35 and S3_130_50. However, the latter
                       had the lowest yield, at 32.5%.

                                   4. Conclusions

                           The aim of the study was to obtain the highest quality, quantity and yield of 316L
                          metal powder for the established atomisation parameters at the assumed process time.
                         Based on the performed characteristics, it was found that:

                                   1.   Torch current and wire feed speed are parameters are parameters that have a sig-
                                    nificant impact on the efficiency of the ultrasonic atomisation process. The highest
                                    efficiency was achieved by the process labelled as S6, with torch current 100 A and
                                 the wire feed speed 9 mm/s.
                                   2.   For some combinations of variable parameters, the atomisation process was highly
                                  unstable. This was manifested by the formation of a mass of liquid metal on the
                               sonotrode surface, which interfered with the correct operation of the ultrasound
                                 generating system.
                                   3.   All performed ultrasonic atomisation processes allowed obtaining powders with
                                   similar and almost spherical grain morphology.
                                   4.   The applied fraction separation method allowed for the separation of powder fractions
                              with grain sizes and PSD dedicated to PBF processes.
                                   5.   After repeated sieving of the powder for all performed atomisation processes, approxi-
                               mately 53% of the fraction with grain size in the range from 50 to 80 ang, approximately
                         36% of the fraction with grain size smaller than 50 µm were obtained.
                                   6.   The chemical compositions of the obtained powders differed slightly from the val-
                              ues described by the standards. The most satisfactory chemical composition was
                                  characterised by the powder marked as S6.

                                Further experimental studies will involve the use of 316L steel powders obtained in
                      LPBF technology. Their aim will be to investigate the influence of the type of material

               Abstract.  In the post-processing of large maritime components, a considerable amount of
                waste in the form of milling and grinding chips  is produced.  At the same time, additive
                manufacturing technologies have shown great potential in producing high-volume parts for
                maritime applications, allowing novel design approaches and short lead times. In this context,
                    this study presents a sustainable approach to recycle and use aluminium bronze waste material,
                 generated during post-processing of large cast ship propellers, as feedstock for laser-powder
                  directed energy deposition.  The recycling technology used to produce powder batches  is
                  inductive re-melting in combination with ultrasonic atomization. The derived metal powders are
                  characterized using digital image analysis, powder flowability tests, scanning electron microscopy
                  as well as energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy.  Compared to conventional metal powders
                produced by gas atomization, the recycled material shows excellent sphericity and a powder
                    size distribution with a higher content of finer and coarser particles. Metallographic sections
                    of deposited additively produced specimens show an increased hardness and reduced ductility,
                but also competitive densities and higher yield and ultimate tensile strength compared to cast
                  material. The process chain shows high potential for the maritime sector to enable circular and
                  sustainable manufacturing.

The alloy offers good material properties and high resistance to cavitation and corrosion in
sea water which makes it especially suitable for maritime applications [1].  After casting and
several machining steps, ship propellers are ground in a dry grinding process to generate the

   There are some authors who investigate the use of metal swarf as feedstock for AM processes.
For example, Jackson et al. [2] produce specimens from ball milled 304L steel machining chips

After heat treatment, the mechanical properties of produced specimens exceed the conventional

   For AM feedstock, the characteristics and properties of the metal powder are very important
for good processability and part quality. In order to analyze the powders, certain characterization
processes can be applied. They often include measurements of PSD, morphology of particles,
flowability or chemical composition.  In the literature, applicable methods and procedures
for characterization are  investigated  extensively.   For example, Wimler  et  al.    [4] and
Mitterlehner et al.  [5] investigate various methods to measure PSD and morphology of AM
powders. Kiani et al. [6] use statistical approaches for powder characterization. The studies of
Baesso et al. [7] and Spierings et al. [8] apply and compare methods of standardized flowability
tests.

4                Agricultural and Rural Development in Denizli, Turkey
                      with Support from the IPARD Program

                                   Cihan Çalıkoğlu1*


1 Department of Economics and Economic Policy in Agribusiness, Faculty of Economics, Poznan University of Life Sciences
* E-mail: [email redacted]


Keywords: rural development, EU-IPARD, TOPSIS, fuzzy methods


This study assesses the EU Instrument for Pre-Accession Assistance for Rural Development (IPARD) on rural
development in Denizli Province, Turkey. The aim of the study is to assess the level and spatial distribution of
IPARD support in Denizli’s rural districts and to examine its relationship with the socio-economic development
profiles of these districts. The analysis integrates secondary data and primary survey data collected from IPARD
beneficiaries (n =86) from a population of 723 projects, where the sample size was determined using a finite
population correction method with a 10% margin of error, and interviews were allocated across districts using
Probability Proportional to Size (PPS) sampling. The methodological framework combines multi-criteria decision-
making and econometric approaches. A socio-economic development index was constructed using the TOPSIS
method based on district-level indicators (H2), while agricultural structures were identified through fuzzy cluster-
ing techniques (H3). IPARD Satisfaction Index was developed using Triangular Fuzzy TOPSIS based on Likert-
scale survey responses (H4). Hypotheses were tested using correlation analysis and ordinary least squares (OLS)
regression (H1–H2), as well as ordered logit modelling (H4).

The results reveal a differentiated spatial distribution of IPARD support across districts. A statistically significant
negative relationship is identified between socio-economic development and per capita IPARD support (H2), in-
dicating that funds are more intensively directed towards less-developed districts, consistent with the program’s
objective. In addition, agricultural districts demonstrate higher engagement with the program in terms of support
per hectare (H3), although investment intensity per project remains lower due to the prevalence of smaller-scale
farms. At the individual level, the relationship between farm size and support is weak and statistically limited (H1).
At the beneficiary level, the findings indicate that individual capabilities are key determinants of program success.
Entrepreneurial initiative and participation in training activities significantly increase the probability of achieving
higher IPARD success levels (H4), while education level is found to have a negative effect on the ordered logit
model (H4). Cooperative membership is also negatively associated with performance outcomes (H4). Qualitative
interview evidence supports this result, suggesting that many cooperatives function only formally (“signboard
cooperatives”) and remain largely inactive in practice. Furthermore, administrative burden and bureaucratic pro-
cedures are identified as key factors negatively affecting beneficiary satisfaction. Overall, the study demonstrates
that IPARD operates as a territorially differentiated policy instrument, contributing both to rural development and
to the redistribution of support towards structurally disadvantaged areas, while highlighting the importance of
individual-level capacities and institutional effectiveness in maximizing program outcomes.

5                   Amyloid-Like Protein in the Enamel Matrix:
           Investigating Sequential and Structural Properties of Amelogenin

                                  Julia Cieszko1*, Małgorzata Kotulska1


1 Department of Biomedical Engineering, Faculty of Fundamental Problems of Technology, Wrocław University of Science
  and Technology
* E-mail: [email redacted]


Keywords: bioinformatics, amelogenin, amyloidogenesis, proteins structure modeling


Amelogenin is a protein found in the enamel matrix during the early stages of tooth development. The protein
exhibits the ability to self-assemble into a stable scaffold for the developing enamel [1]. Microscopic studies show
that the type of structure formed depends on the amino acid composition and the length of the amelogenin isoform.
This is particularly important because the determinants of amyloid formation remain poorly understood, especially
in terms of how sequence context, structural features, and environmental conditions influence different pathways of
aggregation. Amelogenin, due to its ability to adopt different structural forms depending on isoform length and com-
position, provides a valuable model for identifying subtle yet critical factors that drive amyloid assembly. These
structures may take the form of spherical nanodroplets or elongated, structured fibrils resembling amyloids [2, 3].
The formation process is fully controlled by protease activity, in contrast to pathological amyloidogenesis. Once
their function is achieved, the development of the structure is discontinued, and it undergoes degradation [3]. To
investigate the influence of specific protein motifs on the formation of different types of amelogenin aggregates,
a sequence and structural analysis of 38 protein isoforms was performed. Results obtained using AGGRESCAN
4D, Waltz, and AlphaFold 3 enabled the identification of motifs, potentially involved in fibril formation. Interest-
ingly, shorter protein isoforms, which according to the literature form nanodroplets, did not contain these frag-
ments. The factors responsible for the formation of stable nanodroplets remain unknown, however, they are worth
further investigation, particularly in the context of reports suggesting that similar structures may transition into
amyloid fibrils [4]. The structural diversity and controlled nature of the aggregation process make amelogenin
a model molecule for studying factors that determine differences in self-assembly behavior. At the same time,
understanding the mechanisms of functional fibrillation may shed light on the processes distinguishing controlled
from pathological amyloidogenesis, contributing to the development of research aimed at inhibiting disease-related
processes.

6     One- and Two-Photon Excited pH-Modulated Emission of Carbon Nanodots

      Marek Czyszczoń1*, Sebastian G. Mucha1, Leszek M. Mazur1, Katarzyna Matczyszyn1, 2


1 Institute of Advanced Materials, Faculty of Chemistry, Wrocław University of Science and Technology
2 International Institute for Sustainability with Knotted Chiral Meta Matter (WPI-SKCM2), Hiroshima University
* E-mail: [email redacted]


Keywords: carbon nanodots, multiphoton processes, fluorescence-based sensor, pH sensing


Carbon nanodots (CNDs) are a class of fluorescent nanomaterials of sizes smaller than 10 nm. They exhibit fasci-
nating properties, including excellent photostability, biocompatibility, and tunability of light emission [1].

Non-toxic and biocompatible sensors are crucial for in vivo studies. In particular, fluorescent materials that can be
excited via two-photon excitation have the upper hand over typical one-photon excited dyes due to precise locali-
zation and lower photon energy.

Carbon nanodots emitting cyan and yellow light have been developed by thermal decomposition of phloroglucinol,
possessing high fluorescence quantum yields (exceeding 65% and 40%, respectively) and exhibiting two-photon
excited fluorescence [2]. Here, we continue the studies on these nanodots, showing that their fluorescence intensity
can be modulated by changes of the pH of the surrounding medium under both one- and two-photon excitation.
This is the first report of such two-photon excited pH-modulated fluorescence over a wide pH range. These find-
ings provide an excellent and sensitive material for applications in sensing, especially within the physiological pH
range (6.5–8). Moreover, mechanistic studies, including UV-Vis spectroscopy, zeta potential and fluorescence
lifetime measurements, were conducted in order to explain the mechanism of such pH dependence, aiding further
understanding of the nature of this novel nanomaterial.

7    Age-Stratified EEG Synchronization in ADHD: Disentangling Disorder-Specific,
       Developmental, and Pharmacological Effects on Brain Network Dynamics

                             Zofia Dobrowolska1*, Mirosław Łątka1


1 Biomedical Engineering, Department of Fundamental Problems of Technology, Wrocław University of Science and
  Technology
* E-mail: [email redacted]

Keywords: ADHD, EEG synchronization, functional connectivity, neurodevelopment, biomarkers


Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a prevalent neurodevelopmental condition associated with
widespread alterations in brain network organization. Electroencephalography (EEG) offers a non-invasive,
temporally sensitive means of quantifying functional connectivity and large-scale network dynamics – features
known to differ both in ADHD and across normal neurodevelopment. A critical, and frequently underestimated,
methodological challenge is that many EEG synchronization signatures associated with ADHD overlap sub-
stantially with those arising from typical maturation. For instance, theta power decreases by up to 60% between
early adolescence and adulthood in neurotypical individuals, meaning that a pattern indicative of disorder in
one age group may fall within the normative range in another [1, 2]. Disentangling these trajectories is therefore
a prerequisite for the development of new EEG based methods for ADHD detection.

My doctoral research addresses this challenge through a cross-cohort resting-state EEG paradigm spanning
childhood through adulthood. Synchronization between EEG channels is quantified using windowed connec-
tivity measures across the delta, theta, alpha, beta, and gamma bands, yielding dynamic synchronization ma-
trices from which both node-level (mean connectivity, clustering coefficient) and network-level (global effi-
ciency, spectral characteristics) graph-theoretic properties are extracted. Normative age-related trajectories
of EEG synchronization are first established across matched healthy control groups spanning multiple devel-
opmental stages. These lifespan baselines then serve as reference functions against which ADHD-related
deviations are evaluated – permitting the identification of synchronization changes that are genuinely disor-
der-specific rather than reflections of maturational lag or acceleration [3].

Building on this age-stratified framework, the study further isolates pharmacological effects by comparing
connectivity profiles across cohorts that differ in stimulant medication status. Research indicates that com-
monly prescribed methylphenidate-class medications modulate theta/beta ratios and frontal coherence in
ways that can partially normalize – or alternatively mask – disorder-related network signatures [4]. Regional
interactions of particular interest include frontal-parietal and frontal–central connectivity, which have been
implicated in attentional control and executive function deficits in ADHD across age groups [5].

The results are expected to yield age-stratified EEG synchronization norms, disorder-specific network bi-
omarkers distinguishable from both healthy development and pharmacological modulation, and a framework
for interpreting resting-state connectivity measures in the context of neurodevelopmental heterogeneity.

function.arguments:
{"answer": "## Documented cases

The clearest published *metal-run interruption* I found is for 316L stainless steel. The closest copper-alloy report documents incomplete powder recovery and sonotrode contamination, but **not** a witnessed nozzle blockage or melt running off the plate. The distinction matters when diagnosing an individual failed run. (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000029)

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

**Copper-alloy interpretation.** Müller and colleagues atomized nickel–aluminium bronze propeller-grinding chips on an AMAZEMET rePowder system. They attribute the non-powder portion of their 77% recovery mainly to organic and ceramic contamination collected as slag; they do not identify it as metal that escaped the sonotrode. Their 1 mm melt-feed nozzle was chosen *to avoid possible* blockage by residual ceramic abrasive, not to repair a blockage they observed. They did observe carbon fibres in the product and attributed them to hot melt detaching fibres from the woven carbon-fibre sonotrode. Their proposed change to another sonotrode material, ideally similar to the alloy, was **not tested** in that report. The paper says the *chips* received no cleaning or purification before or after atomization; that statement is **not** a procedure for cleaning the sonotrode. (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019)

**Metal accumulation and reduced yield.** Bałasz and colleagues stopped five of sixteen planned 316L ATO Lab arc-and-wire atomizations—S5, S9, S10, S13 and S14—after unstable operation formed a mass of liquid metal on the sonotrode that interfered with the ultrasonic system. They considered excessive wire feed and/or insufficient arc current the likely parameter mismatch. Selecting an appropriate feed/current combination was their operating remedy: S6, at **100 A and 6.83 mm/s**, returned **80.6%** powder; S3, at 130 A and 18.82 mm/s, returned 32.5%. These are **different parameter settings**, not evidence that a second run on a reused plate yielded less. Nor do the authors establish that resonance itself was lost. The paper’s conclusion rounds the preferred feed to approximately 9 mm/s, but its methods identify S6 precisely as 6.83 mm/s; the separate 100 A, 9.47 mm/s run S2 returned 66.0%. (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000032)

**Useful diagnostic analog, not a metal report.** In a laboratory study intended to inform future liquid-metal experiments, Szostak-Staropiętka and colleagues atomized *nonmetal surrogate liquids* on a 160 × 30 × 1 mm adjustable stainless-steel plate. Partial atomization initially left a patterned liquid buildup: measured vibration amplitude reached only about **2.8 µm**, despite higher generator settings drawing more power. Rearranging the acoustic-amplifier configuration produced **8 µm** and smooth atomization of the ordinary surrogate. A much more viscous surrogate still built up instead of atomizing; turning ultrasound off let it drain down the plate. These observations support checking **measured plate displacement**, rather than assuming a generator percentage proves adequate vibration, but do not establish a cause or fix for an actual metal runoff or lost-resonance incident. The authors say a metal-capable stand remained future work. The publication’s cropped Figures 8, 10 and 11 show the retained-liquid pattern, recovered atomization and high-viscosity buildup, respectively. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028)

## Published placement, inclination and maintenance guidance

- **Where the stream lands:** Kustron and colleagues’ *proposed* metal-atomizer design directs the molten stream **onto the vibrating working surface** and sizes that surface to capture as much of the stream as possible while preserving sufficiently high, well-distributed amplitude. For their broad twin-wire-arc-spray stream, they chose a **140 mm** plate as a compromise: smaller plates offered greater central displacement but could miss part of the stream; a 190 mm plate covered it but had lower displacement. This is design guidance, **not** an experimentally validated rule to aim a narrow crucible-fed stream at a particular distance from the centre, rim, node or antinode. Their reported water tests and modelling should not be represented as failed molten-metal trials. (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000023)
- **Inclination:** Szostak-Staropiętka and colleagues simulated one droplet at **30°, 45° and 60°** plate inclination. After 0.004 s, respectively **48.2%, 49.7% and 50.9%** of the initial liquid area remained: a 2.7-percentage-point spread. They judged that small for *one simulated droplet*, while cautioning that inclination may matter at greater feed rates and for apparatus geometry and heat transfer. Their physical stand allowed adjustment. These results do **not** prescribe an optimum tilt for molten aluminium bronze. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000016)
- **Between-run cleaning and replacement:** I found **no documented protocol** in these primary reports for scraping, chemically cleaning or replacing a metal-atomization plate between runs, and no controlled clean-versus-reused-plate yield comparison. Müller and colleagues’ suggestion to change sonotrode *material* addresses shed carbon fibres, not a demonstrated between-run replacement schedule. Bałasz and colleagues describe vacuuming and blowing **powder sieves** between sieving portions; this must not be mistaken for sonotrode cleaning. (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005)

**Evidence gap:** Among the accessible reports examined, I could not verify a first-hand copper- or aluminium-alloy account that explicitly records unatomized melt running from the plate into the collector, a lower-yield second run caused by plate reuse, an actual melt-feed nozzle clog, or measured loss of acoustic resonance. The sources above instead document slag-associated recovery loss, sonotrode-derived contamination, liquid-metal accumulation interrupting 316L runs, and a separate surrogate-liquid amplitude failure; their proposed and demonstrated fixes should not be conflated. (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000012)"}

rePOWDER, or laboratory ultrasonic atomizers) where a run partly failed: melt that did not atomize and
ran off the plate or sonotrode into the collector, solid build-up on the plate, lower yield on a
second run with a reused plate or sonotrode, nozzle clogging, or loss of resonance. Prefer copper
alloys, aluminum bronze or other aluminum-containing melts. For each report give the alloy, set-up,
the cause the authors identified and the fix. Also report any published guidance on where the melt
stream should land on the plate, on plate inclination, and on how plates are cleaned or replaced
between runs.

No. ## Documented cases

The clearest published *metal-run interruption* I found is for 316L stainless steel. The closest copper-alloy report documents incomplete powder recovery and sonotrode contamination, but **not** a witnessed nozzle blockage or melt running off the plate. The distinction matters when diagnosing an individual failed run. (muller2023usingultrasonicatomization pages 3-6, muller2023usingultrasonicatomization pages 6-8, bałasz2024aninvestigationof pages 2-4, bałasz2024aninvestigationof pages 9-11)

(2023), CuAl10Ni5Fe5 nickel–aluminium bronze**; DOI: 10.1088/1757-899X/1296/1/012036 | AMAZEMET **rePowder**; graphite crucible/pouring system; 1 mm nozzle; woven, binder-free carbon-fibre sonotrode at 40 kHz; argon; 1300 °C. Powder yield was **77%**; the balance was mainly slag containing organic and ceramic contamination. Carbon fibres detached from the sonotrode and entered the powder. (muller2023usingultrasonicatomization pages 3-6, muller2023usingultrasonicatomization pages 6-8) | The 1 mm nozzle was selected to reduce the **risk** of clogging by residual ceramic abrasive; the paper does **not** report an actual clog. Hot-melt exposure caused carbon fibres to detach from the sonotrode. (muller2023usingultrasonicatomization pages 3-6, muller2023usingultrasonicatomization pages 6-8) | Proposed—not demonstrated—fix: use a sonotrode of another material, ideally compositionally similar to the alloy. No plate cleaning/replacement procedure, runoff event, resonance loss, or reused-plate comparison was reported. (muller2023usingultrasonicatomization pages 6-8) |

(szostakstaropietka2025influenceofprocess pages 11-13) | Rearranging the waveguide/amplifier settings raised amplitude to **8 µm**, after which the ordinary surrogate atomized smoothly; the very-high-viscosity surrogate still built up. contexts.context: This excerpt describes the ultrasonic plasma atomization (UPA) apparatus and mechanisms but does not provide the requested first-hand reports of partial failures. It mentions high-speed optical imaging of resting liquid droplets on a vibrating plate, and a UPA configuration in which a plasma torch melts feedstock on a horn-coupled sonotrode. The process uses ultrasonic vibration, capillary waves, acoustic cavitation, and plasma heating to detach and atomize molten metal. In the macroscopic setup, droplets are directed downstream to a cooled surface or capture ring, where they quench into powder. The excerpt does not identify a specific failed alloy run or document unatomized molten metal collecting or running off the plate, solid/melt buildup, a second low-yield run using a reused plate, nozzle clogging, resonance loss, plate tilt, stream landing location during a failure, or actual cleaning/replacement corrective actions. It therefore offers apparatus context relevant to the search, but no qualifying incident report or detailed failure-and-correction account.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides a first-hand report of ultrasonic atomization of 316L stainless steel wire using an ATO Lab atomizer. The process melts 1.2 mm-diameter wire with an electric arc; the melt lands on a sonotrode connected to an ultrasound generator, is atomized by ultrasound, and is carried by high-pressure argon. The reported apparatus settings included torch current from 70–150 A, wire-feed speed from 35–60%, constant argon flow of 60%, ultrasonic amplitude of 80%, and frequency of 35.0–35.3 kHz. Five of sixteen planned runs (S5, S9, S10, S13, and S14) exhibited high instability. The authors attributed this most likely to unsuitable parameter combinations, particularly excessive wire-feed speed or insufficient torch current, and discontinued those runs. However, the excerpt does not describe the specific failure modes requested: unatomized melt collecting or running off the plate, solid/melt buildup, plate tilt, stream landing location, plate cleaning or replacement, reuse of a plate with low yield, nozzle clogging, or loss of resonance. It also reports no corrective action beyond stopping the unstable experiments.
contexts.question: Find first-hand reports of ultrasonic atomization of molten metals on vibrating plates or sonotrodes with partial failures: unatomized molten metal collecting or running off plate, buildup of solid/melt on platform, second run with reused plate low yield, melt-delivery nozzle clogging, loss of resonance. Specify alloy, apparatus, cause and actual corrective action; report stream landing location, plate tilt, plate cleaning/replacement.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides a first-hand report of partial failure during ultrasonic atomisation of molten 316L stainless steel. The apparatus used a sonotrode platform connected to an ultrasound generator; molten 316L was produced using an electric arc and deposited on the sonotrode, where ultrasound ejected it and a high-pressure argon flow atomised it. Under the low-current/high-wire-speed parameter combination, a considerable amount of molten metal accumulated on the sonotrode platform. The buildup prevented the ultrasound system from operating properly, causing some atomisation runs to be interrupted. The study identifies torch current and wire-feed speed as significant process parameters and reports the highest efficiency at 100 A torch current and 9 mm/s wire-feed speed. The supplied pages do not state that the melt ran off the plate, identify a nozzle clog, document loss of resonance specifically, describe a second run using a reused plate, or report a corrective action such as cleaning or replacing the sonotrode. They also do not provide the stream landing location or plate tilt. Thus, this is evidence of molten-metal buildup and operational interruption, but not of the other requested failure details.

contexts.context: The excerpt documents several firsthand process failures and their remedies. In the first run, liquid deposited on the vibrating plate in a pattern matching the vibration nodes and antinodes rather than atomizing; additional droplets increased the residual layer thickness and absorbed power, but the liquid did not flow off because the vibration energy was insufficient. Laser and micrometer measurements found a maximum converter amplitude of only about 2.8 µm, with output reaching 2.4 µm over the generator setting range of 5–60% and 2.8 µm at 70%; higher settings produced no meaningful amplitude increase despite greater power consumption. The remedy was to rearrange the waveguiding-signal-amplifier settings, raising amplitude to 8 µm, after which atomization proceeded smoothly and was strongest at the plate nodes (Figure 10). A liquid specified at 7.5 mPa·s viscosity, 997 kg/m³ density, and 0.055 N/m surface tension required at least 8 µm amplitude. For a very high-viscosity liquid, insufficient amplitude caused buildup and no atomization; switching ultrasound off allowed the pattern to spread and drain as a stream, while switching it on recreated the pattern. This excerpt does not provide the requested alloy identity, collection method, nozzle obstruction, resonant-frequency, plate-tilt/pouring-position, cleaning details, or numerical yield.

contexts.context: A 2025 *Metrology* laboratory study used a vibrating plate fed through a calibrated 2-mm orifice (1 drop/s to continuous stream). In the first run, liquid accumulated in node/antinode patterns and did not atomize or run off because measured amplitude was only 2.8 µm; a liquid of viscosity 7.5 mPa·s required at least 8 µm. Rearranging waveguiding-signal amplifiers raised amplitude to 8 µm and atomization proceeded, strongest at nodes. For high-viscosity liquid, buildup persisted until ultrasound was switched off, when it spread and flowed downward. No alloy, plate inclination, landing-location, cleaning, or replacement guidance is given.

contexts.context: Kustron et al. (2023) describe the melt stream as being directed onto the surface of the vibrating plate coupled to the ultrasonic transducer. The plate diameter was selected to capture as much of the converging molten stream as possible, rather than specifying that impact should occur at the center or edge. Their design objective was also to maintain high and uniform vibration amplitude across the working surface. The numerical analysis explicitly distinguishes nodal points, where amplitude is zero, from locations of maximum deflection; therefore, the excerpt supports avoiding nodal points for effective atomization, but it does not identify a preferred center-versus-edge impact position. contexts.context: This excerpt from Szostak-Staropiętka et al. (2025) provides experimental evidence about vibration amplitude and locations of atomization on a vibrating plate, but it does not describe a published metal-melt apparatus design in sufficient detail to answer all parts of the question. In the experiment, the initial measured maximum amplitude was only about 2.8 µm, which was insufficient to initiate atomization; after amplifier settings were rearranged, an amplitude of 8 µm was reached and atomization proceeded smoothly. The authors observed that atomization was strongest at the nodes of the vibrating plate, rather than at antinodes. For a liquid with viscosity 7.5 mPa·s, density 997 kg/m³, and surface tension 0.055 N/m, the required amplitude was at least 8 µm. The excerpt does not state whether a melt stream should strike near the center or edge of the plate, nor does it provide instructions concerning plate inclination angle, regular abrasive cleaning, removal of adherent metal, or replacing plates between runs. It also concerns liquid atomization experiments and simulations, not powder characterization. The paper’s conclusion supports ultrasonic atomization as potentially applicable to testing liquid properties, including liquid metals, while emphasizing that simulations can identify experimental problems such as overestimated output amplitude.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides experimental and simulation evidence relevant to plate inclination and vibration-mode effects, but it does not establish where a melt stream should strike the plate—near its center or edge—or whether impact should be placed specifically at an antinode or nodal point. The apparatus used an adjustable inclined vibrating surface, specifically a 160 mm × 30 mm × 1 mm stainless-steel plate. Simulations compared 30°, 45°, and 60° inclinations after 0.004 s. The experiment did observe that residual liquid formed a pattern corresponding to the plate’s nodes and antinodes, demonstrating that the vibration mode affects liquid retention and distribution. answer.formatted_answer:
Question: Find reports of ultrasonic atomization of metals (plate or sonotrode atomizers such as the AMAZEMET
rePOWDER, or laboratory ultrasonic atomizers) where a run partly failed: melt that did not atomize and
ran off the plate or sonotrode into the collector, solid build-up on the plate, lower yield on a
second run with a reused plate or sonotrode, nozzle clogging, or loss of resonance. Prefer copper
alloys, aluminum bronze or other aluminum-containing melts. For each report give the alloy, set-up,
the cause the authors identified and the fix. Also report any published guidance on where the melt
stream should land on the plate, on plate inclination, and on how plates are cleaned or replaced
between runs.


No. ## Documented cases

The clearest published *metal-run interruption* I found is for 316L stainless steel. The closest copper-alloy report documents incomplete powder recovery and sonotrode contamination, but **not** a witnessed nozzle blockage or melt running off the plate. The distinction matters when diagnosing an individual failed run. (muller2023usingultrasonicatomization pages 3-6, muller2023usingultrasonicatomization pages 6-8, bałasz2024aninvestigationof pages 2-4, bałasz2024aninvestigationof pages 9-11)

| Report and alloy | Set-up and observed outcome | Author-identified cause | Fix, status, and evidentiary limits |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Müller et al. (2023), CuAl10Ni5Fe5 nickel–aluminium bronze**; DOI: 10.1088/1757-899X/1296/1/012036 | AMAZEMET **rePowder**; graphite crucible/pouring system; 1 mm nozzle; woven, binder-free carbon-fibre sonotrode at 40 kHz; argon; 1300 °C. Powder yield was **77%**; the balance was mainly slag containing organic and ceramic contamination. Carbon fibres detached from the sonotrode and entered the powder. (muller2023usingultrasonicatomization pages 3-6, muller2023usingultrasonicatomization pages 6-8) | The 1 mm nozzle was selected to reduce the **risk** of clogging by residual ceramic abrasive; the paper does **not** report an actual clog. Hot-melt exposure caused carbon fibres to detach from the sonotrode. (muller2023usingultrasonicatomization pages 3-6, muller2023usingultrasonicatomization pages 6-8) | Proposed—not demonstrated—fix: use a sonotrode of another material, ideally compositionally similar to the alloy. No plate cleaning/replacement procedure, runoff event, resonance loss, or reused-plate comparison was reported. (muller2023usingultrasonicatomization pages 6-8) |
| **Bałasz et al. (2024), 316L stainless steel**; DOI: 10.3390/ma17225642 | **ATO Lab** arc/wire atomizer; 35.0–35.3 kHz, 80% amplitude, constant argon setting, 60 min runs. Runs S5, S9, S10, S13 and S14 were stopped for instability. Liquid-metal mass accumulated on the sonotrode and impaired ultrasound operation. Best recovery was **80.6%** for S6: 100 A, 35% feed = **6.83 mm/s**. S2—100 A, 40% = **9.47 mm/s**—gave **66.0%**; S3—130 A, 50% = **18.82 mm/s**—gave only **32.5%**. (bałasz2024aninvestigationof pages 2-4, bałasz2024aninvestigationof pages 9-11, bałasz2024aninvestigationof media d6621dff) | Authors attributed instability to an unsuitable current/feed combination—particularly excessive wire feed or insufficient current—so melting outpaced atomization, thickening the liquid layer and interfering with the ultrasonic system. (bałasz2024aninvestigationof pages 2-4, bałasz2024aninvestigationof pages 9-11) | Demonstrated operating remedy: match feed to melting capacity; among tested settings, S6 was most efficient. The yield differences were between parameter sets, **not** first and second runs on a reused sonotrode. *Table: Comparison of directly documented metal-atomization problems and one clearly separated surrogate-liquid failure. The table distinguishes observed events and tested remedies from preventive design choices, proposed fixes, and requested failure modes that were not reported.*

**Copper-alloy interpretation.** Müller and colleagues atomized nickel–aluminium bronze propeller-grinding chips on an AMAZEMET rePowder system. They attribute the non-powder portion of their 77% recovery mainly to organic and ceramic contamination collected as slag; they do not identify it as metal that escaped the sonotrode. Their 1 mm melt-feed nozzle was chosen *to avoid possible* blockage by residual ceramic abrasive, not to repair a blockage they observed. They did observe carbon fibres in the product and attributed them to hot melt detaching fibres from the woven carbon-fibre sonotrode. Their proposed change to another sonotrode material, ideally similar to the alloy, was **not tested** in that report. The paper says the *chips* received no cleaning or purification before or after atomization; that statement is **not** a procedure for cleaning the sonotrode. (muller2023usingultrasonicatomization pages 3-6, muller2023usingultrasonicatomization pages 6-8)

**Metal accumulation and reduced yield.** Bałasz and colleagues stopped five of sixteen planned 316L ATO Lab arc-and-wire atomizations—S5, S9, S10, S13 and S14—after unstable operation formed a mass of liquid metal on the sonotrode that interfered with the ultrasonic system. They considered excessive wire feed and/or insufficient arc current the likely parameter mismatch. Selecting an appropriate feed/current combination was their operating remedy: S6, at **100 A and 6.83 mm/s**, returned **80.6%** powder; S3, at 130 A and 18.82 mm/s, returned 32.5%. These are **different parameter settings**, not evidence that a second run on a reused plate yielded less. Nor do the authors establish that resonance itself was lost. The paper’s conclusion rounds the preferred feed to approximately 9 mm/s, but its methods identify S6 precisely as 6.83 mm/s; the separate 100 A, 9.47 mm/s run S2 returned 66.0%. (bałasz2024aninvestigationof pages 2-4, bałasz2024aninvestigationof pages 9-11, bałasz2024aninvestigationof media d6621dff)

**Useful diagnostic analog, not a metal report.** In a laboratory study intended to inform future liquid-metal experiments, Szostak-Staropiętka and colleagues atomized *nonmetal surrogate liquids* on a 160 × 30 × 1 mm adjustable stainless-steel plate. Partial atomization initially left a patterned liquid buildup: measured vibration amplitude reached only about **2.8 µm**, despite higher generator settings drawing more power. Rearranging the acoustic-amplifier configuration produced **8 µm** and smooth atomization of the ordinary surrogate. A much more viscous surrogate still built up instead of atomizing; turning ultrasound off let it drain down the plate. These observations support checking **measured plate displacement**, rather than assuming a generator percentage proves adequate vibration, but do not establish a cause or fix for an actual metal runoff or lost-resonance incident. The authors say a metal-capable stand remained future work. The publication’s cropped Figures 8, 10 and 11 show the retained-liquid pattern, recovered atomization and high-viscosity buildup, respectively. (szostakstaropietka2025influenceofprocess pages 8-11, szostakstaropietka2025influenceofprocess pages 11-13, szostakstaropietka2025influenceofprocess pages 13-15, szostakstaropietka2025influenceofprocess media 4b1fed1b, szostakstaropietka2025influenceofprocess media 591a7a70, szostakstaropietka2025influenceofprocess media 950c9656)

## Published placement, inclination and maintenance guidance

- **Where the stream lands:** Kustron and colleagues’ *proposed* metal-atomizer design directs the molten stream **onto the vibrating working surface** and sizes that surface to capture as much of the stream as possible while preserving sufficiently high, well-distributed amplitude. For their broad twin-wire-arc-spray stream, they chose a **140 mm** plate as a compromise: smaller plates offered greater central displacement but could miss part of the stream; a 190 mm plate covered it but had lower displacement. This is design guidance, **not** an experimentally validated rule to aim a narrow crucible-fed stream at a particular distance from the centre, rim, node or antinode. Their reported water tests and modelling should not be represented as failed molten-metal trials. (kustron2023developmentofhighpower pages 2-4, kustron2023developmentofhighpower pages 4-7, kustron2023developmentofhighpower pages 7-10)
- **Inclination:** Szostak-Staropiętka and colleagues simulated one droplet at **30°, 45° and 60°** plate inclination. After 0.004 s, respectively **48.2%, 49.7% and 50.9%** of the initial liquid area remained: a 2.7-percentage-point spread. They judged that small for *one simulated droplet*, while cautioning that inclination may matter at greater feed rates and for apparatus geometry and heat transfer. Their physical stand allowed adjustment. These results do **not** prescribe an optimum tilt for molten aluminium bronze. (szostakstaropietka2025influenceofprocess pages 8-11, szostakstaropietka2025influenceofprocess pages 5-8, szostakstaropietka2025influenceofprocess pages 13-15)
- **Between-run cleaning and replacement:** I found **no documented protocol** in these primary reports for scraping, chemically cleaning or replacing a metal-atomization plate between runs, and no controlled clean-versus-reused-plate yield comparison. Müller and colleagues’ suggestion to change sonotrode *material* addresses shed carbon fibres, not a demonstrated between-run replacement schedule. Bałasz and colleagues describe vacuuming and blowing **powder sieves** between sieving portions; this must not be mistaken for sonotrode cleaning. (muller2023usingultrasonicatomization pages 6-8, bałasz2024aninvestigationof pages 4-7, bałasz2024aninvestigationof pages 2-4)

**Evidence gap:** Among the accessible reports examined, I could not verify a first-hand copper- or aluminium-alloy account that explicitly records unatomized melt running from the plate into the collector, a lower-yield second run caused by plate reuse, an actual melt-feed nozzle clog, or measured loss of acoustic resonance. The sources above instead document slag-associated recovery loss, sonotrode-derived contamination, liquid-metal accumulation interrupting 316L runs, and a separate surrogate-liquid amplitude failure; their proposed and demonstrated fixes should not be conflated. (muller2023usingultrasonicatomization pages 3-6, muller2023usingultrasonicatomization pages 6-8, bałasz2024aninvestigationof pages 2-4, bałasz2024aninvestigationof pages 9-11, szostakstaropietka2025influenceofprocess pages 11-13)

info.query:
Find reports of ultrasonic atomization of metals (plate or sonotrode atomizers such as the AMAZEMET
rePOWDER, or laboratory ultrasonic atomizers) where a run partly failed: melt that did not atomize and
ran off the plate or sonotrode into the collector, solid build-up on the plate, lower yield on a
second run with a reused plate or sonotrode, nozzle clogging, or loss of resonance. Prefer copper
alloys, aluminum bronze or other aluminum-containing melts. For each report give the alloy, set-up,
the cause the authors identified and the fix. Also report any published guidance on where the melt
stream should land on the plate, on plate inclination, and on how plates are cleaned or replaced
between runs.
